text: Volcanic ash in Kansas, it's true there's thick deposits of this stuff there, but
where are the source volcanoes? Geologists began puzzling over this in the late
1800s when these deposits were first recognized. We're coming to you today from
the Rock Chemistry Laboratory at the Cascades Volcano Observatory of the US
Geological Survey, and it's in places like this that geological mysteries like
that of the Kansas ash gets solved. Now initially it was thought that the ash
came from northern New Mexico. That's the direction of the prevailing winds,
and of course there are lots of volcanoes in northern New Mexico, but the
chemistry of the ash didn't match the chemistry of the rocks. There wasn't a
good match with the rocks in Long Valley Caldera, another big explosive volcanic
system located in eastern California, but Yellowstone, spot-on match, not only in
terms of the rock chemistry, but also in the timing. These ash beds in Kansas
and throughout the Great Plains matched up with the big caldera forming
eruptions from 2.1 million years ago, 1.3 million years ago, and 631,000
years ago. And these deposits have been found throughout the West, in fact even
offshore of northern California in marine sediment drill cores. And it's not
just these most recent three eruptions that have deposited ash across the
landscape. Past Yellowstone system eruptions have done that as well. The
ashfall fossil beds in Nebraska are made up of ash from a 12 million year
old volcanic eruption when the Yellowstone hotspot was in southern
Idaho. We're going to learn an awful lot about the Yellowstone system by
looking at ash that covers the western United States. Alright, well that's the
story from Kansas. Now let's head back to Yellowstone and talk about ground
deformation, seismicity, and geyser activity that occurred during the month
of February. February continued to see background levels of seismicity in the
Yellowstone region. The University of Utah located 125 earthquakes in the area
during the month. The largest was a magnitude 2.6 event that occurred on
February 23rd, just to the north of Yellowstone Lake. There were also two
swarms during the month. One included 49 events in the vicinity of Norris Geyser
Basin, and the other included 15 events just to the north of West Yellowstone
Montana. Those both occurred in this area where we see a lot of the seismicity
in the Yellowstone region between Hebgen Lake and the north central part of
Yellowstone National Park. Turning now to ground deformation, this is vertical
deformation at the White Lake GPS station on the east side of the
caldera. It spans two years. Each one of these blue dots is one day worth of
data. Downward trends indicate subsidence, the ground sinking, and upward
trends indicate uplift or rising of the ground. And the trends we're seeing over
this two-year period are the same things we've seen since 2015. That the
ground subsides at a few centimeters, an inch or two per year, and it's
interrupted in the summertime by a little bit of uplift or at least a
pause as groundwater is recharged from snow melt and spring runoff. Now since
about September or so of last year, we've seen about two and a half
centimeters, a little over an inch of subsidence, so we're really just
continuing the trends that have been going on now for nine years. Finally
looking at the tallest geyser in the world, steamboat geyser. This is the
temperature measured in the runoff channel of the geyser. All of this
little spiky activity are minor eruptions and then we had our first
major eruption of the year in the early morning hours of February 26th
and then it dropped back down to background temperatures. So steamboat
remains active, one eruption so far in 2024. Well that's the YVO update
